title: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
body:
### Problem

Many applications require long-running functions. In many cases, `[USER].cache_data` and `[USER].cache_resource` will suffice to achieve good performance, but these are not suitable when the inputs to the function change very frequently. 

One common sub-case of this is where the output of the function is important, but not time critical. In this case it would be good to render the page and then "fill-in" the missing parts when the function finishes running.

### Solution

**MVP:** What's the smallest possible solution that would get 80% of the problem out of the way?

I propose a decorator `st.run_in_background` that returns a spinner (like the `st.cache_resource` decorator) while a function is running, but does not block the execution of the application. 

To illustrate the idea:

```python
[USER].run_in_background(show_spinner='Generating the plot')
def plot_data(data):
    '''Just an example of a slow function'''
    return sns.pairplot(data)

def get_results(data):
    '''Just an example of a fast function'''
    return 'All good' 

st.title('My app')

selected_data = ... # let's assume this changes a lot, eg. due to interactive filters
results = get_results(selected_data)

fig = plot_data(selected_data ) # This is slow to run
st.pyplot(fig)

st.write(results)
```

In the code above, it'd be great if `st.pyplot` displayed a spinner while `plot_data` is executing (without blocking `st.write(results)`) and then "fill-in" the space with the plot once `plot_data` finishes executing.

**Possible additions:** What are other things that could be added to the MVP over time to make it better?

Smart error handling to turn any operation on a "delayed" object would be very cool.

For example, in this code:

```python
fig = plot_data(data)
fig.update_axes(...) # this would error if fig is not a matplotlib figure, it'd be awesome if streamlit could figure out this is still being loaded without blocking execution
```

### Additional context

Ultimately I'm proposing that streamlit replicate the lazy loading as done in PowerBI (for example)

![image](https://apps.provingground.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/08/Tracer-OfficeSpaceDash.gif)

Note that every chart is "loading separately" as far as the users are concerned. 


---

### Related Issues

[Joining user threads](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5826)
[Trigger a script re-run from another thread](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/2838)

---

Community voting on feature requests enables the Streamlit team to understand which features are most important to our users.

**If you'd like the Streamlit team to prioritize this feature request, please use the 👍 (thumbs up emoji) reaction in response to the initial post.**

```python
import streamlit as st 
import time
import functools 
import threading

class ResultThread(threading.Thread):
    """
    A custom Thread that can return the value of the function 
    runned inside it
    """
    fx_output = None
    error = None

    def run(self, *args, **kwargs):
        try:
            if self._target:
                self.fx_output = self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)
        except Exception as e:
            self.error = e
        finally:
            del self._target, self._args, self._kwargs

    def await_output(self):
        """
        Wait for the thread to finish and return the return value of fx
        """
        self.join()
        return self.fx_output

    def get_error(self):
        """
        Return error if any, return None if no error occured
        """
        self.join()
        return self.error

def threaded(daemon=False):
    """
    A decorator to run a function in a separate thread, this is useful
    when you want to do any IO operations (network request, prints, etc...)
    and want to do something else while waiting for it to finish.
    :param fx: the function to run in a separate thread
    :param daemon: boolean whether or not to run as a daemon thread
    :return: whatever fx returns
    """
    def _threaded(fx):
        [USER].wraps(fx)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            thread = ResultThread(target=fx, daemon=daemon,
                                  args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
            thread.start()
            return thread
        return wrapper

    return _threaded
```

Hey all — this issue has been on my radar and I wanted to share some design thinking. Sharing it here since this issue already captures the problem well and I'd love to get reactions.

### The idea: `st.background_task`

A managed API for kicking off long-running work that survives reruns:

```python
task = st.background_task(slow_query, args=(params,), key="my_query")

if task.running:
    st.info("Query running...")
elif task.done:
    st.dataframe(task.result)
```

The `key` deduplicates across reruns (same key = same task, not a new one). When the task finishes, the runtime automatically triggers a rerun so you can render the result — no polling needed. Tasks get cleaned up when the session ends.

The workaround [USER] shared above with raw threads works, but threads created outside Streamlit don't have access to `ScriptRunContext`, can't trigger reruns on completion, and aren't tied to the session lifecycle. This would handle all of that.

### How it relates to parallel fragments

We're working on `[USER].fragment(parallel=True)` ([#14277](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14277)) which gives concurrency *within* a single script run — independent UI sections load at the same time. Background tasks would be different: the work outlives reruns, produces data rather than UI, and doesn't block interactions. They'd be complementary.

### Open questions

- Does the API shape feel right? The original proposal here used a decorator (`[USER].run_in_background`) — any preference?
- What are your actual use cases? Long queries, model training, batch jobs?
- How important is cancellation when inputs change?

Would love to hear what people think.

An update here: now that we have the features of `st.cache_data(refresh_mode="background")` and `st.fragment(parallel=True)` there is a pattern for this combining these. 

See the app that I have created here illustrating how to use these for long-running tasks: https://long-query-patterns.streamlit.app/
See also this PR updating our skills: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17446

Note, there is a gap associated with this that has surfaced while testing this pattern, when you have a user interaction with an element that is inside a fragment, that will not interrupt the main run and will need to wait for the long running task to complete. I created an issue to track this here: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17445 . If this is affecting your use case, please upvote and comment on that issue. Please let me know if you have any other use cases which this suggested pattern does not address 🙏
